messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 24.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo energy harvester: sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25 nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20 MOhm).
    *   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a storage capacitor at node `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out,avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (settled)
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6) vary in $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, and $R_L$.
    *   Crucial observation: $V_{oc,peak} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (nominal). This is quite low. Diode drops (even Schottky $\sim 0.25\text{ V}$) significantly impact efficiency.

    *   Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) fails on S2 (heavy load, $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{ V}$), S3 (strong excitation, $V_{max} > 3.6\text{ V}$), S4 (weak excitation, $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{ V}$), and S5 (settled).
    *   Issues with FBR:
        1.  Diode voltage drops limit the output voltage, especially for low $I_p$ (S4).
        2.  No voltage regulation (S3 over-voltage).
        3.  Passive rectification is inefficient for low-amplitude signals.

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* Uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks. This significantly increases the harvested energy.
    *   *Active Rectification:* Replaces diodes with switches. However, the `SYNC` controller given is specifically designed for peak-switching (like SSHI), not as a general-purpose active bridge.
    *   *Zener Clamping:* To prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding 3.6 V.
    *   *Voltage Multipliers:* Usually too lossy for these low-voltage piezos.

    *   The available `SYNC` controller closes switches at piezo voltage extrema.
    *   A classic SSHI implementation involves an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ that shorts the piezo (pzp, pzn) or is placed in series with a rectifier.
    *   Actually, the most effective SSHI variant for low-voltage sources is the "Parallel-SSHI" or "Series-SSHI". Let's consider a Parallel-SSHI: The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$. When the switch closes at the peak, it creates an LC oscillation that flips the voltage on $C_p$, effectively reducing the voltage the piezo has to "fight" against and increasing current flow into the rectifier.
    *   Wait, the simplest SSHI implementation is:
        1.  Full-bridge rectifier (DSCH) to charge $C_{out}$.
        2.  An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo terminals (`pzp`, `pzn`).
        3.  The switch $S$ closes at the peaks (both edges) for $t_{on} \approx \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{L C_p}$ (Wait, the prompt says $\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$, let's stick to the prompt's hint).

    *   Let's refine the SSHI topology:
        *   $D1, D2, D3, D4$ as a full bridge.
        *   $C_{out}$ at the output.
        *   $L1$ and $S1$ in parallel with the piezo (pzp to pzn).
        *   Wait, if the switch $S1$ just shorts the piezo through $L1$, it's the "Parallel-SSHI" technique.
        *   Wait, the FBR is `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        *   Wait, the piezo terminals are `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   If $S1$ is between `pzp` and `pzn` with $L1$ in series, it's a shunt.
        *   Let's try:
            - Full Bridge: $D1(\text{pzp}, \text{out})$, $D2(\text{pzn}, \text{out})$, $D3(0, \text{pzp})$, $D4(0, \text{pzn})$.
            - Shunt: $L1(\text{pzp}, \text{n1})$, $S1(\text{n1}, \text{pzn})$.
            - Controller: $G1$ (SYNC), `edges: both`, `ton` optimized.
            - Storage: $C_{out}(\text{out}, 0)$.
            - Protection: $D_{zener}(\text{out}, 0)$ (no, the prompt says `["0", "out"]` for zener clamp). Let's add a $DZ33$ from `0` to `out`.

    *   *Correction on Zener:* $DZ33$ breakdown is 3.3 V. If we put $DZ33$ as `["0", "out"]`, the cathode is at `out`. It conducts when $V_{out} > 3.3\text{ V}$. This fits $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   S2, S4 (low power): SSHI increases power significantly.
    *   S3 (high power): $DZ33$ limits $V_{out}$.
    *   S5 (low frequency): SSHI is generally frequency-independent as long as $t_{on}$ is scaled (and SYNC does this).
    *   Ripple: $C_{out}$ will be tuned.
    *   Startup: SSHI speeds up $C_{out}$ charging.

    *   $D1, D2, D3, D4$ (DSCH)
    *   $L1$ (Value to be tuned, e.g., $10\text{ mH}$)
    *   $S1$ (Connected to $G1$)
    *   $G1$ (SYNC, `edges: both`, `ton` to be tuned)
    *   $C1$ (Storage, $2.2\text{ \mu F}$ as a starting point)
    *   $D_{zener}$ (DZ33, `["0", "out"]`)
    *   Total components: $4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 9$ (well within 16).

    *   `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1)
    *   `pzn` $\to$ `out` (D2)
    *   `0` $\to$ `pzp` (D3)
    *   `0` $\to$ `pzn` (D4)
    *   `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (L1)
    *   `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (S1)
    *   `out` $\to$ `0` (C1)
    *   `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33)
    *   `G1` (SYNC) controlling `S1`

    Wait, let's double check the rectifier nodes.
    Full bridge:
    - Diode 1: `pzp` to `out`
    - Diode 2: `pzn` to `out`
    - Diode 3: `0` to `pzp`
    - Diode 4: `0` to `pzn`
    Wait, this is a standard bridge?
    Current flow:
    - When $V_{pzp} > V_{pzn}$ and $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$: $pzp \to out$. Current return? $0 \to pzn$.
    - When $V_{pzn} > V_{pzp}$ and $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$: $pzn \to out$. Current return? $0 \to pzp$.
    Yes, this is the standard full-bridge config.

    Let's refine $t_{on}$. For $L=10\text{ mH}, C_p=25\text{ nF}$, $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \sqrt{250 \cdot 10^{-12}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 15.8\text{ \mu s} \approx 50\text{ \mu s}$.

    *   $D1$: `["pzp", "out"]`, DSCH
    *   $D2$: `["pzn", "out"]`, DSCH
    *   $D3$: `["0", "pzp"]`, DSCH
    *   $D4$: `["0", "pzn"]`, DSCH
    *   $L1$: `["pzp", "n1"]`, $10\text{ mH}$
    *   $S1$: `["n1", "pzn"]`, ctrl: `G1`
    *   $G1$: `SYNC`, `ton=50u`, `edges="both"`, `phase=0`
    *   $C1$: `["out", "0"]`, $2.2\text{ \mu F}$
    *   $D_{zener}$: `["0", "out"]`, DZ33

    *   S2/S4 (Low voltage): Parallel-SSHI increases the voltage across the bridge by effectively multiplying the charge available at each half-cycle.
    *   S3 (High voltage): DZ33 limits $V_{out}$ to $\sim 3.3\text{ V}$, which is $< 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   $V_{pp}$: Large $C1$ reduces ripple.
    *   $t_{up}$: Faster charging due to SSHI.

    Wait, should the Zener be on `out`? Yes, the prompt says "zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out)". This is exactly what I have.

    Let's double check if I can use a more efficient SSHI. Parallel-SSHI is the most common for this. The switch $S1$ is placed in parallel with the piezo. When it closes, it creates an $L-C_p$ resonant circuit.

    Actually, let's reconsider the bridge. Is there a way to avoid two diode drops?
    The prompt mentions `S` switches. I could potentially build a synchronous rectifier, but the `SYNC` controller is very specific about "piezo voltage extrema" and "ton". It's not designed for a bridge. It's designed for SSHI.

    One more thing: $C_p$ is nominal $25\text{ nF}$, but in S6 it's $30\text{ nF}$. The $t_{on}$ might need adjustment, but the evolution strategy will handle the value tuning.

    Final check on the components:
    - D1, D2, D3, D4 (DSCH)
    - L1 (L)
    - S1 (S)
    - G1 (SYNC)
    - C1 (C)
    - DZ1 (D, DZ33)
    Total = 9 components.

    Wait, the $L$ series resistance is $2\text{ Ohm} + 5\text{ Ohm/mH}$. For $10\text{ mH}$, $R_s = 2 + 50 = 52\text{ Ohm}$. This is small compared to the piezo impedance.

    Let's check the "edges" and "phase".
    `edges: both` means the switch closes at both the positive and negative peaks. This is correct for Parallel-SSHI.
    `phase: 0` means it closes exactly at the peak.

    One final check on the Zener:
    $DZ33$ breakdown is $3.3\text{ V}$. The requirement is $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$. $3.3\text{ V}$ is safe.

    Wait, is $t_{on}$ provided in seconds? Yes. $50\text{ \mu s} = 50\text{e-6}$.

    Wait, a thought: Should the inductor $L1$ be in series with the rectifier? No, Parallel-SSHI is usually a shunt. Let's stick to that.

    Let's double check the Zener direction again.
    `["0", "out"]` $\implies$ anode at `0`, cathode at `out`.
    Current flows from anode to cathode if forward biased (meaning `out` is negative), or from cathode to anode if reverse biased above $V_{BR}$.
    Since `out` is positive, it is reverse biased. When $V_{out} > 3.3\text{ V}$, it conducts from `out` to `0`, clamping the voltage. This is correct.

    Is there any other way to improve?
    If the power is still too low for S4, the only other option is a different SSHI topology (like Series-SSHI), but that requires more components and a more complex interface. Parallel-SSHI is usually sufficient.

    Wait, let's re-verify the bridge diodes' model. `DSCH` is the low-drop Schottky. Good.
